doc.title: Ray Drummond interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Why he left American business: shrinking time horizons at Allstate
summary: He recounts the five-year plan culture at Allstate in 1968-70 giving way to weekly numbers, and criticizes corporate greed and Enron.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: reasons that I left the business world, left Stanford, was something that I actually had seen at Allstate while I was there. I was there from ’68 to ’70, for two years, and I left because I could not believe the short attention span that was now developing in American business. When I first got to Allstate in ’68 one of the most important parts of the company in their planning effort was they looked at a five year plan and a ten year plan, and those — the five year plan was in service of the ten year plan so the annual plan was in service of the five year plan, but the five year plan was the most important. The ten year plan was important too, and the one year plan was important to get to the five year plan. But the most important thing was the five year plan. By the time I left Allstate in September of 1970 the quarter was not even as important as each week. See in our monthly — well not monthly — but in our weekly Monday morning meeting, because you have to understand Allstate Insurance Company, there’s a region, this is the region, it’s not a district office or anything, the Menlo Park Regional Office which is Northern California, and Sacramento had the rest of California and Nevada so I had to cover both of those regions. Anyway the point was I’d go to the Menlo Park meeting because that was my home gig. By the time I left our weekly meeting would generally have all the managers trying to make their numbers look the best for the previous week, and the estimates for this coming week were more important than what they were estimating for the month, the quarter, the year, five years, what? What? What is that? Ten years. Who ever heard? What? Ten years exists? And so it’s like I saw that and I said it’s over. American business is finished. There’ll be creative this and that but as far as creating anything, you don’t run a business day to day. The businesses run because you have a vision, still you’re a creative person but you’re a businessperson. And businesspeople don’t just make money, they make the money because they have something that somebody wants, and somebody wants it not because you’re forcing it down their throat, somebody wants it because they can use it. It’s something that’s made well, that somebody wants. And they’re going to go out and get it. Now that upsets traditional marketing — now you want to say traditional, I’d say marketing since the fifties, since the post war. Because post war everybody’s now thinking they’ve been taught all these wonderful concepts about how to manipulate mass markets and how to influence people through media manipulation and this and that. And it works for a time but eventually it runs out of gas for each product. So when you have a product that’s not made well and it’s forced down people’s throats, eventually it peters out. Now a product that’s made well that’s priced well, that stands up, that the company stands behind continues on. I mean it does. There’s no question, even if the product is obsolete, people will still vote to use that product because it works, it’s convenient, it’s priced well. American business is like — and it’s an infection that’s going around the rest of the world. I mean the Japanese

resisted as long as they could but they’re — and it’s not even about money either, that’s what makes it so sad, because ultimately it’s really not about how much we made or how much we didn’t make, it’s really about how much did we give to our stockholders. And that’s such a game that’s being played. I mean we see the results of that game, and right now there’s a big cover-up going on because it’s not about what happened to Enron and those guys it’s about what’s going on with the rest of all these jacklays, as James Williams says, yeah everybody’s trying to figure out a way that they can make sure they can cover up all their tracks. Because everybody’s been doing the exact same things as all these other companies. I mean that’s what they’ve been teaching in business school.
